section_summary: This section documents U.S. wartime monitoring of Japanese diplomatic, commercial, propaganda, and suspected espionage activity across Latin America. Major subjects include intercepted correspondence, the Japan Tourist Bureau’s government-financed propaganda program, Japanese interest in strategic minerals and petroleum, and alleged intelligence networks operating through Mitsui-related firms in Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, and Ecuador. It also contains State Department circulation records and assessments of an OSS study of Japanese communities in Latin America.

subfiles.title: Summary of Japanese Messages
subfiles.doc_type: FBI transmittal memorandum with translation summary
subfiles.from: J. Edgar Hoover, Director, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.to: Adolf A. Berle Jr., Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Transmits an FBI Translation Section summary of fifteen Japanese business and personal letters photographed by the U.S. Embassy in Buenos Aires.
subfiles.summary: Summary of thirty-four photographed sheets (fifteen letters, September 20-October 2, 1942) of a Japanese firm's business correspondence; FBI found no clear subversion.

subfiles.title: Instruction No. 3606 concerning filmed Japanese correspondence
subfiles.about: Forwards the government’s summary of Japanese messages filmed by the embassy and discourages risky collection efforts.
subfiles.summary: Instruction No. 3606: the filmed correspondence is judged insufficiently valuable to justify risks; future films welcome if easily accessible.

subfiles.title: Japanese Radio Group
subfiles.from: J. Edgar Hoover, Director, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.to: Adolf A. Berle Jr., Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Reports a Japanese diplomatic intercept concerning Axis travel controls and South American boundary-defense negotiations.
subfiles.summary: Intercepted October 9 message from Japan's ambassador in Argentina on a Montevideo conference decision to regulate Axis nationals' movements and Brazilian-Uruguayan boundary defense.

subfiles.title: Italian, German and Japanese Diplomatic Radio Messages
subfiles.about: Indexes a memorandum reporting the results of an examination of Axis diplomatic radio messages.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to a Justice memorandum on Italian, German and Japanese diplomatic radio traffic (R62.20210/2064).

subfiles.title: Osaka Syosen Kaisya, São Paulo, Brazil
subfiles.from: J. Edgar Hoover, Director, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.about: Reports that a Japanese shipping-company manager photographed Rosario’s port facilities in 1940.
subfiles.summary: Source: Osaka Shosen Kaisha's Sao Paulo manager and Buenos Aires colleagues photographed Rosario's port, wharves and grain depots in December 1940, though the firm had no office there.

subfiles.title: Japanese-German sabotage plan, “36”
subfiles.about: Indexes a Peruvian despatch enclosing three embassy memoranda on an alleged Japanese-German sabotage plan.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: three memoranda on a Japanese-German sabotage plan '36' (800.20210/1451).

subfiles.title: Alleged German and Japanese military plan affecting Central and Latin American republics
subfiles.about: Indexes a Justice Department memorandum on an alleged Axis military plan concerning Latin America.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to a Hoover memorandum on an alleged German-Japanese military plan affecting Central and Latin American republics (800.20210/1458).

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 9366: Japan Tourist Bureau—Organization
subfiles.from: U.S. Embassy, Buenos Aires; Hugh Millard for the Ambassador
subfiles.about: Forwards translated internal papers describing the Japan Tourist Bureau’s organization, budget, and propaganda program.
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 9366: the 1941 Japan Tourist Bureau program, funded by Japanese government money, with over half its ¥1.56 million devoted to propaganda; its Buenos Aires office links to Tsuda and the Japanese Embassy.

subfiles.title: Items Connected with Policy for Project Activities in 1941
subfiles.from: Tateo Tsutsumi, Japan Tourist Bureau Buenos Aires office
subfiles.to: Takanori Kimura, Permanent Director, International Tourist Bureau, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Proposes an expanded, locally adapted Japanese propaganda campaign in South America.
subfiles.summary: Tsutsumi recommends a permanent Rio representative and more Spanish printed matter, films and exhibitions, cultural content to reach Argentine papers, and invitations to journalists and second-generation Japanese.

subfiles.title: Japan Tourist Bureau’s Budget Plan for 1941
subfiles.about: Lists projected receipts and expenditures for the 1941 fiscal year, including overseas offices and propaganda activities.
subfiles.summary: The budget anticipates receipts of ¥1.56 million, principally from a government subsidy and Railway Special Accounts. Expenditures include ¥425,000 for ten overseas offices and ¥843,000 for propaganda, covering publications, films, advertising, broadcasting, exhibits, agents, invitations, and delegated work. It also raises planning-investigation spending sharply, chiefly for research into expanding propaganda.

subfiles.title: Details and Application of the 1941 Budget Plan
subfiles.about: Explains how the Bureau’s 1941 receipts and appropriations were to be administered and used.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum details financing, staffing, rent, travel, and operating allowances for offices from New York and Buenos Aires to Berlin, Manila, and Hanoi. It describes coordinated propaganda under the Tripartite Pact, multilingual publications and films, advertising allocations, part-time agents, commissioned work, invitations, and distribution expenses. The document also provides for propaganda-expansion research and for cooperation in spy prevention within the East Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere.

subfiles.title: Analysis of Material Contained in the Takano File
subfiles.from: Donald R. Heath, Counselor of Embassy, Santiago
subfiles.about: Assesses seized Compañía Chilena Oriental records for evidence of Japanese intelligence activity and interest in strategic materials.
subfiles.summary: Takano File analysis: Chilean Oriental's expelled manager Miyasaki was a dangerous spy; the records show interest in strategic minerals and munitions and contact with agent Moreno Echevarria, but not Pearl Harbor foreknowledge.

subfiles.title: Department of State routing sheet
subfiles.from: Department of State, Under Secretary Liaison Office
subfiles.about: Records internal routing among numerous State Department offices.
subfiles.summary: Routing sheet with office abbreviations and a February 25 stamp; no narrative.

subfiles.title: Japanese Press Propaganda Using Statements of Allied Prisoners
subfiles.about: Translates a pro-Axis Chilean newspaper article presenting alleged statements by captured American and British naval officers.
subfiles.summary: Naval intelligence translates an El Chileno article attributing claims of Japanese naval superiority and Allied errors to captured officers Donovan and Cooper, as propaganda for Chilean readers.

subfiles.title: Transmission of “Field Notes on the Japanese in Latin America”
subfiles.from: William L. Langer, Director, OSS Research and Analysis Branch
subfiles.to: Philip W. Bonsal, Department of State
subfiles.about: Sends the State Department a confidential OSS study of Japanese communities in Latin America.
subfiles.summary: Langer sends OSS Research and Analysis Report No. 791, 'Field Notes on the Japanese in Latin America'.

subfiles.title: Instruction transmitting “Field Notes on the Japanese in Latin America” to Mexico
subfiles.about: Forwards Robert B. Hall’s confidential OSS report to the embassy in Mexico.
subfiles.summary: Instruction sends Mexico the OSS report by Colonel Robert Hall, from a mid-1942 field trip.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of OSS report
subfiles.about: Acknowledges receipt of the OSS report on Japanese people in Latin America.
subfiles.summary: Bonsal formally acknowledges receiving “Field Notes on Japanese in Latin America.” The letter contains no substantive evaluation of the study.

subfiles.title: Assessment of OSS report “Field Notes on the Japanese in Latin America”
subfiles.to: Philip W. Bonsal and Mr. Dreier
subfiles.about: Evaluates the usefulness of Robert B. Hall’s study and highlights its discussion of Okinawans in Peru and Brazil.
subfiles.summary: Memo finds little new in the OSS report but praises its summary of Japanese immigration, economics and controls, and Hall's suggestion to exploit Okinawan resentment.

subfiles.title: Instruction transmitting “Field Notes on the Japanese in Latin America” to Brazil
subfiles.about: Forwards Robert B. Hall’s confidential OSS report to the embassy in Brazil.
subfiles.summary: Instruction sends Brazil the OSS report by Hall as possibly of interest.

subfiles.title: Compania Minero Petrolera del Pacifico—Republic of Ecuador
subfiles.from: J. Edgar Hoover, Director, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.to: Adolf A. Berle Jr., Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Forwards intelligence concerning an Ecuadorian petroleum company suspected of Japanese financial connections.
subfiles.summary: Hoover sends a memorandum on Compania Minero Petrolera del Pacifico in Ecuador, also supplied to embassies in Quito and Bogota.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Compañía Minero Petrolera del Pacífico
subfiles.about: Reviews conflicting reports that Japanese interests financed or controlled a large Ecuadorian oil concession.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum identifies the company’s officers, concession in Esmeraldas, and proposed sale to International Petroleum Company, while emphasizing the absence of conclusive proof of Japanese ownership. Other sources allege that Japanese representatives financed the concession, hired geologists, and made payments through Suganami and Nakamura in Bogotá. Detailed background on Suganami and Luis Martinez Delgado connects them with Japanese commercial, intelligence, Nazi, or Fascist circles, but the memorandum concludes that further investigation is required.

subfiles.title: Transmittal concerning the JAPSA case
subfiles.from: J. Edgar Hoover, Director, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.to: Adolf A. Berle Jr., Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Forwards a restricted memorandum on an alleged Japanese espionage ring operating through commercial firms in South America.
subfiles.summary: Hoover reports a Buenos Aires-Rio-Santiago network allegedly forwarding information to Japan, to be undisclosed without authorization, distributed to five embassies.

subfiles.title: JAPSA Case: Compañía Chilena Oriental and Nambei Trading Company
subfiles.to: Department of State and U.S. intelligence agencies
subfiles.about: Describes an alleged Japanese espionage network operating through Mitsui-related companies and covert correspondence in Argentina, Brazil, and Chile.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum argues that Japanese nationals used Spanish cover names and small commercial firms to funnel intelligence to the Japanese Embassy in Buenos Aires after Chile broke relations with the Axis. It profiles personnel of Compañía Chilena Oriental, including Isao Takada, Kaname Nakayama, Goro Miyasaki, Takeo Takano, Susuki Nakatsuka, Takeo Ozasa Tanaka, and S. Hagiwara, detailing alleged photography, mapping, financial, propaganda, and intelligence activities. It also describes the Nambei Trading Company and reproduces clandestine addressing instructions using aliases and intermediaries such as S. Miura and Francisco Ortiz. The surviving excerpt ends mid-discussion of Ortiz’s role in transmitting correspondence.
